blocks.content: docker exec runs a new process inside a container that is already running. It does not create a new container, it reaches into an existing one.

Unlike docker run, which always creates something new, docker exec requires a container that is already running, and starts an additional process inside that same isolated environment, sharing its filesystem, network, and process namespace.

blocks.alt: exec reaches into a container that is already alive

blocks.content: 2. The Key Distinction from docker run
blocks.text: 2. The Key Distinction from docker run

blocks.content: This is one of the most common points of confusion for people new to Docker: docker run image always starts a brand new container, while docker exec container command runs an extra process inside a container that is already up, it never creates anything new.

blocks.alt: run creates something new, exec reaches into what already exists

blocks.content: 3. The Classic Use Case: an Interactive Shell
blocks.text: 3. The Classic Use Case: an Interactive Shell

blocks.content: By far the most common use of exec is popping open an interactive shell inside a running container to look around, check a config file, or debug something live, exactly as if you had SSH'd into it.

blocks.alt: A live shell, inside an already-running container

blocks.content:
docker exec -it web bash
# Drops you into an interactive bash shell running
# inside the already-running "web" container.
root@a1b2c3d4:/# ls /etc/nginx/

blocks.content: 4. You Can exec Multiple Times, Independently
blocks.text: 4. You Can exec Multiple Times, Independently

blocks.content: Nothing about exec is exclusive, you can open several separate exec sessions into the same running container at once (one checking logs, another inspecting files), and none of them affect the container's main process at all.

blocks.alt: Multiple independent exec sessions into the same container

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: docker exec runs a new process inside an already-running container, it never creates a new one, that is what docker run is for.
The most common use is an interactive debugging shell into a live container, effectively "SSH-ing in" without an SSH server.
